query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of aluminum (on the order of 2–4 at.%) to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale during high‐temperature service, thereby significantly increasing its oxygen resistance without sacrificing its high-temperature yield strength or room-temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C but has poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of Al (approximately 2–4 at.%) into the alloy composition during melting/casting.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) at around 1000 °C over prolonged periods (e.g., 100 hours) with concurrent mechanical loading tests that sample the same stress/strain range as current performance benchmarks.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum, having a high affinity for oxygen, preferentially oxidizes to form Al2O3—a well‐known protective oxide at high temperatures. This scale acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress, thereby improving the alloy’s oxidation resistance while leaving the high-temperature mechanical microstructure intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-modified alloy will show a substantially reduced oxidation rate and lower oxide weight gain during high-temperature exposure, while maintaining the original yield strength at 1000 °C and room-temperature tensile ductility within a similar range (8–16%).
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits poor oxygen resistance at elevated temperatures, limiting its practical high-temperature applications despite its useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is valid if the enhanced oxidation resistance is achieved under high-temperature (around 1000 °C) air exposure, and the alloy’s key mechanical properties (tensile ductility of 8–16% at room temperature and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) are not degraded beyond acceptable tolerances.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration and processing conditions must be determined experimentally to ensure that the protective scale forms effectively without introducing harmful intermetallic phases or precipitates that could affect ductility or high-temperature strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: a control batch of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a test batch modified with 2–4 at.% Al. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation tests in air at 1000 °C for 100 hours. Additionally, perform standardized tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C to assess ductility and yield strength. Use surface analytical techniques (e.g., SEM, XRD) to characterize the oxide scale.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and phase composition (via SEM, XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant (e.g., >25% reduction) decrease in oxidation weight gain or shows degradation in yield strength or ductility by more than ±10% relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
